# Introduction

Large extracellular electrophysiological recordings provide invaluable information about neuronal activity and interactions. However, for this information to be uncovered, a good spike sorting is necessary, assigning detected electrical events to putative neurons. In this process, numerous issues could potentially arise. The sorter could confuse neurons, miss spikes, or create spurious units. Such mistakes would naturally impact downstream scientific interpretation, for example, the firing rate and population structure. Classic validation work was done manually. This was not only tedious but also demonstrated that spike separation errors can vary significantly even under careful analysis. For over a decade now, the field has relied on quantitative quality metrics (Harris et al.,2000; Hill et al., 2011\) and often a hard threshold to determine whether a sorted unit should be considered well-isolated or not. 

The challenge lies in that the most meaningful quality targets require ground truth data for each neuron. Ground truth data provides the information to identify **fpos**, which measures the fraction of spikes assigned to a unit that should not be there, and **fmiss**, which measures the fraction of true spikes the sorted unit didn’t capture. In this thesis, both fpos and fmiss will be targets we aim to predict. A model capable of doing this would be practically useful as it would assist in quantifying the risk of over-counting and under-counting neuronal activity. However, training such a model would require extensive ground-truth data, ideally using paired recordings that provide the most realistic ground-truth targets. Yet, paired recordings are rare and costly, and each recording only supplies a single ground-truth unit. Conversely, hybrid simulations are plentiful and comprehensively labelled, but they are not identical to real deployment data.

This asymmetry turns our prediction of fpos and fmiss into a transfer learning challenge. The key question then becomes: can supervision from hybrid simulation data be effectively transferred to real paired recordings? The main task would be for the model to learn using hybrid simulations as our large labelled source domain, then adapt to realistic noise and feature distributions using a small labelled target set plus a large unlabeled target pool, and evaluate our model under strict recording-disjoint protocols that would mimic real operational use.

This thesis lies at the intersection of computational neuroscience, benchmark design, and low-label machine learning.  Neuroscience allows us to identify the problem, define our features and our targets fmiss and fpos, benchmarking practice to decide what constitutes an honest test, and machine learning to compare the different ways to leverage our datasets.

## Research Questions and Hypotheses

The thesis is organised around four hypotheses that reflect the most significant uncertainties.

1. Hybrid and paired data are strongly shifted, making naive source-only transfer insufficient for reliable quality prediction.  
2. Leakage-safe recording context add meaningful predictive signal.  
3. Our targets fpos and fmiss are structurally different prediction targets.  
4. The best model depends on the dataset family and evaluation regime rather and bein an universal model across all paired recordings.

H1 questions the existence of a meaningful transfer problem that would require methods more complex than source-only. H2 tests whether information at the recording level can add significant signal. H3 and H4 move beyond performance and question the heterogeneity of our targets as well as whether different models perform better under different paired recording families. 

## Contributions

The main contributions of the thesis are as follows.

* It constructs a leakage-safe benchmark for predicting spike-sorting error metrics, using recording-disjoint and family-disjoint splits as its main evaluation method, rather than mere unit-level random splits.  
* It quantifies the hybrid-to-paired-domain shift, showing near-perfect domain separability.   
* It compares multiple families of transfer methods, including source-only transfer, context-aware stacking, unlabeled target structure, waveform-enriched stacking, neural baselines based on SSL and MMD.   
* It shows a clear target asymmetry: fpos reveals a significant signal and meaningful transfer, while fmiss shows greater instability.   
* It demonstrates that paired-domain family structure matters. The best fpos model differs across paired recording families.

These contributions are deliberately scoped and do not claim to fully solve the quality control problem. 

## Why does this thesis focus on quality prediction rather than spike sorting end-to-end?

End-to-end spike sorting and post hoc quality estimation are related but distinct problems. First, from a noisy recording signal across multiple channels, neuronal activity, or “spikes,” needs to be identified. Then a spike sorter will group the detected spikes into sets of putative neurons, whose accuracy can range from perfectly accurate to fully erroneous, with spikes misassigned, missed, or attributed to spurious units. Between those two situations exists a continuous spectrum of intermediate levels of sorting accuracy. The quality predictor comes after that sorting stage to identify where each specific putative neuron lies on the spectrum. 

State-of-the-art spike sorters have already drastically improved their performance over the last few decades, as they have been the main focus of the spike sorting field. Post-hoc quality estimation is not yet up to date with all the discoveries in both computational neuroscience and machine learning. This discrepancy highlights the necessity for more resilient, data-driven methods for post-hoc quality evaluation. A reliable quality predictor would improve scientific analysis and curation and could later help understand what constitutes a “good” neuron, which could support the next generation of spike sorting algorithms.

# Literature Review

## History of spike sorting

Monitoring the activity of specific neurons has been an area of research for over half a century. The first neuron’s activity was recorded using glass micropipettes and metal electrodes (Hubel & Wiesel, 1962). At the time, identifying single spikes was a manual job performed by expert operators (Hubel & Wiesel, 1962). Single-neuron activity can be detected with a single electrode and a simple threshold detector built into the hardware. However, the high level of background noise from other neurons in the local area, with action potentials of similar shape and size, made it challenging to isolate a specific neuron’s activity (Lewicki, 1998). The introduction of principal component analysis (PCA) established it as the standard method for feature extraction in spike sorting. It marked the transition from manual methods to a software pipeline composed of four steps: detection, feature extraction, clustering, and evaluation (Lewicki, 1998).

Since the beginning of extracellular recordings, our capacity to monitor multiple neurons simultaneously has doubled every 7 years (Stevenson & Kording, 2011). To capture more and more neural activity, the hardware had to evolve. Starting from micropipettes and a singular metal electrode (Hubel & Wiesel, 1962\) to modern high-density probes (Jun et al, 2017). For the new generation of probes to achieve its full potential, it must be accompanied by the development of adapted spike-sorting algorithms and quality metrics (Einevoll et al., 2012). With more neuronal activity recorded, additional challenges emerged: the signal became harder to parse, and classic sorting algorithms had to evolve to leverage the quantity of information provided by the new hardware.

## Post-hoc analysis in spike sorting

### Manual sorting

Spike sorting has traditionally depended on manual intervention and often still does. Experts inspect waveform clusters one channel at a time, in a two-dimensional PCA projection, and manually define cluster boundaries (Wood et al., 2004). In an experiment led by Wood et al. (2004), five sorting experts were asked to perform manual spike sorting on 20 real motor-cortex channels and five realistic synthetic channels that experts could barely differentiate. The sorting experts agreed only 25% of the time on the number of units in the real channel and had an average error rate of 23% for false positives and 30% for false negatives in synthetic channels (Wood et al., 2004).

This experience demonstrated that manual spike sorting is highly variable, even amongst expert researchers, making it more difficult to draw conclusions from such data.

### Manual Curation

As spike sorting became more automated, manual sorting disappeared. However, experts still perform manual curation tasks to improve performance, such as correcting the putative units identified by the sorters by merging split clusters, verifying cluster assignments, or rejecting poor-quality units (Rossant et al., 2016).

However, manual curation is viewed as a limitation. As it is not a scalable solution (Rossant et al., 2016\) and cause major reproducibility issues in the field (Buccino et al.,2022). 

Recently, Fehér et al. (2025) proposed to automate unit curation using *AECuration*, an autoencoder-based approach trained to separate true neural events from non-neural detections. 

Furthermore, Jain et al. (2025) introduced *UnitRefine*, a community toolbox that uses supervised learning to classify putative units into three categories: noise, single-unit activity, and multi-unit activity. They trained the model using labels assigned by expert curators, whose predictions can vary and may deviate from the ground truth.

### Metrics

Robust quality metrics are vital for determining whether a unit identified by the spike-sorting algorithms corresponds to a single neuron. They are used by manual curators and scientists to assess the reliability of putative units. Quality metrics in spike sorting can be stratified into five categories: isolation (clustering), completeness, contamination, stability (drift), and additional metrics. 

Isolation metrics for clustering, such as isolation distance (Harris et al., 2001), L-ratio (Schmitzer‑Torbert et al., 2005), D-prime (Hill et al., 2011), and silhouette score (Rousseeuw, 1987), are used to quantify how well a putative unit is separated from other units and noise. 

Contamination metrics, such as interspike interval (ISI) (Hill et al., 2011), sliding refractory period violations (Banga et al., 2025), noise cutoff (Laboratory, International Brain., 2022), and signal-to-noise ratio, measure if the algorithm includes noise or spikes from *other* neurons in this cluster; in other words, it measures false positives. 

Completeness metrics, such as amplitude cutoff (Hill et al., 2011), amplitude median (Laboratory, International Brain, 2022), amplitude coefficient variation, and presence ratio, measure if the algorithm fails to see some spikes that actually belong to this neuron; in other words, it measures false negatives. 

Drift metrics, such as drift peak-to-peak (Siegle et al., 2021), drift standard deviation (Siegle et al., 2021), and drift median absolute deviation (Siegle et al., 2021), quantify the physical stability of a neuron relative to the recording electrodes. 

Quality metrics are insightful but not sufficient to distinguish with perfect precision which putative units are accurate. In fact, they are proxies while we aim to estimate the ground-truth error rate. 

## Different Spike sorting algorithms

Spike sorters' families differ in their structure and what they optimise for. Template-based methods are among the most popular; they use spike waveforms, which serve as the signature of a neuron to determine the unit to which a spike belongs. From this group, we will evaluate KiloSort (Pachitariu et al., 2016), KiloSort2, SpyKING CIRCUS (Yger et al., 2018), and Klusta (Rossant et al., 2016). This approach particularly excels at resolving overlapping spikes and scales effectively to high-dimensional probes. Similarly, JRClust (Jun et al., 2017\) and its extension, IronClust (Jun et al., 2020), were designed for high-density probes, and their algorithms account for potential probe drift to prevent assignment errors. HerdingSpikes2 (Hilgen et al., 2017\) combines spatial localisation with waveform features for dense multielectrode arrays, while MountainSort4 (Chung et al., 2017\) has a fully automated pipeline designed for reproducible spike sorting. Finally, Tridesclous (Garcia & Pouzat, 2019\) can run online or offline and prioritises integration over new algorithmic discoveries. 

These spike sorters differ in terms of the probes they are designed for, the edge cases they consider, their robustness, their need for manual curation, and how they handle overlapping spikes. All of these factors influence how they will sort spikes across different units. Therefore, a recording sorted by different sorters might yield different numbers of detected spikes or neurons.

## Machine learning

### Transfer learning and domain shift

Transfer learning is a machine learning approach where knowledge gained from one task or domain is reused to enhance performance on a different, yet related, task or domain (Pratt et al., 1991). When data is limited, transfer learning offers an excellent way to train a model on synthetic data and subsequently adapt it to real-world data. For instance, Zhang et al. (2022) describe their sim-to-real setting as related to supervised domain adaptation for few-shot learning, where only very few labelled target samples are available, and report strong performance. This motivates the idea that applying the same transfer learning from synthetic spike sorting data to real paired recordings could improve our model. 

### Tabular data regression

For small to medium tabular datasets, tree-based methods often outperform neural networks.  Grinsztajn et al. (2022) demonstrated that tree-based models remain state-of-the-art on tabular datasets with around 10, 000 rows.  For example, XGBoost, introduced by Chen and Guestrin (2016), is very effective for small datasets due to its sparsity-aware algorithm.

## Research Gap

Extensive research has been carried out to improve sorters and benchmark their performance. Meanwhile, we continue to assess the quality of putative units using proxy metrics. Some experiments have been conducted to identify noise units and multi-unit activity units through human curation data (Jain et al., 2025). However, classification does not fully capture small variations in unit quality, and even expert curators sometimes make mistakes, which can make the labels unreliable.

To the best of our knowledge, no previous work has attempted to predict the two continuous variables, fpos and fmiss, which are part of the neuron accuracy formula, using a supervised learning regression model.

# Data and Methodology

## Dataset Taxonomy and Benchmark Scope

The thesis relies solely on SpikeForest (Magland et al., 2020\) as its source of information. SpikeForest is a benchmarking framework that assesses multiple spike sorters using ground-truth datasets. It is the largest source of ground-truth data, offering recordings from various laboratories, probes, and types, including paired juxtacellular recordings, simulations, and hybrid simulations. Using the hybrid simulation recordings and the paired juxtacellular recordings they provided, we constructed a dataset where each row represents a putative unit with four columns for its features and two for target fmiss and fpos. The final dataset contains 33,206 rows from 61 recordings and 9 spike sorters. Of these rows, 24,224 come from hybrid simulations and 8,982 come from paired juxtacellular recordings. However, out of the 8,982, only 207 paired rows have a label. In paired juxtacellular settings, only one neuron can be monitored per recording. The high-dimensional probe captures multiple neurons, so the sorter detects several of them, but only one ground truth can be monitored. The remaining 8,775 are putative units detected by the sorters that help us understand the context of recording as well as the underlying structure of paired recordings data.

### Paired juxtacellular recordings

![][image1]  
**Figure 1\. Paired juxtacellular and extracellular recording setup. A juxtacellular electrode records ground-truth spikes from a single neuron, while a high-density probe simultaneously captures extracellular activity from surrounding neurons across multiple channels, enabling evaluation of spike-sorting accuracy.**

Paired juxtacellular recordings are comprised of two sensors. First, a probe with multiple channels meant to record the activity potential of nearby neurons. Channels are close to each other, and the activity of a single neuron often overlaps across multiple channels. The recordings dataset is a multivariate time series represented as a matrix, where each row is indexed by a timestamp and each column corresponds to the recorded voltage for a specific channel. 

The juxtacellular electrode, on the other hand, is a glass micropipette recording from a single neuron. Its recording dataset is represented as a two-column matrix, with the first column indexing rows by timestamps and the second column recording high-amplitude voltage traces. Its proximity to the neuron’s membrane allows it to capture almost every single action potential from 1-10mV range, while multi-channel probes might detect them from 100-500µV. This capacity to capture every signal from a single target neuron is what makes it a legitimate ground truth.

### Hybrid simulations

As mentioned in the litterature review, one of the main challenges of the field is to obtain quality ground truth data. Simulated dataset became very popular for benchmarking sorters but they can only be so close to reality. In order to paliate to it hybrid simulation datasets emerged.  Hybrid datasets are constructed by combining a real extracellular recording with artificially reinserted real neuronal spike waveforms whose spike times and identities are known exactly.

This approach offers two main advantages. First, it preserves the multi-channel noise structure and waveform variability. Second, it provides exact spike-time ground truth, enabling rigorous evaluation of the developed quality metrics. In contrast to synthetic simulations, they employ a realistic noise model and, unlike purely in vivo recordings, allow performance measurement.

The primary assumption underlying hybrid simulations is that the reinserted templates accurately represent neuronal extracellular signatures under stationary recording conditions. The limitations of hybrid simulations include a potential underrepresentation of extreme waveforms and tha most neurons selected have a high signal-to-noise ratio.

### What kind of dataset each spilt component is

* Hybrid labelled source data: These rows are the main supervision reservoir used in the transfer learning process to teach the learning of a specific task.  
* Paired labelled target data: These rows are scarce but are the most scientifically significant. They are used both to evaluate our model on the test set and to train our model. In our model, transfer learning methods are used to adapt the model to the target domain.  
* Paired unlabeled target data: these rows can’t be used for supervised learning. However, they preserve the structure of the target domain. They are useful for support estimation, pseudo-label selection, and representation learning. The rows coming from the held-out recordings should remain excluded from any interpretation. 

### Datasets origins

#### Paired datasets

Five families of paired data recording were included in our dataset, PAIRED\_BOYDEN from Allen et al. (2018), PAIRED\_CRCNS\_HC1by Henze et al. (2000) and Harris et al. (2000), PAIRED\_ENGLISH from English et al. (2017), PAIRED\_KAMPFF published by Neto et al. (2016) and Marques-Smith et al. (2018), and PAIRED\_MEA64C\_YGER published by Yger et al. (2018) and Spampinato et al. (2018). They were accessed from the SpikeForest benchmark framework (Magland et al., 2020), which standardises probe geometry and has already run multiple spike sorting algorithms with accessible results. 

PAIRED\_BOYDEN. Drawn from Allen et al. (2018), this study set contains in vivo patch-clamp recordings paired with high-density extracellular arrays (32–256 channels) in mouse cortex. It is particularly informative for characterising how neuronal bursting modulates spike waveform shape across a train — a known confound for template-matching sorters. No canonical repository record with an explicit data licence was identified; licence status should be confirmed with the authors prior to any redistribution.

PAIRED\_CRCNS\_HC1. Originally published by Henze et al. (2000) and Harris et al. (2000), this legacy dataset consists of simultaneous intracellular and extracellular recordings from the CA1 hippocampal region of anaesthetised rats, using wire tetrodes and 6-site linear silicon probes. It is hosted on CRCNS.org and subject to its terms of use: scientific purposes only, no public redistribution, with mandatory attribution to the authors and the repository.

PAIRED\_ENGLISH. Contributed by English et al. (2017) from the Buzsáki laboratory, this study set comprises 29 paired recordings from awake behaving mice spanning hippocampus, neocortex, and thalamus, using a hybrid probe with a juxtacellular electrode glued directly atop a NeuroNexus silicon probe at approximately 20 µm separation. These recordings are distributed via the SpikeForest API; no external repository record with an explicit data licence was identified, and licence status should be confirmed with the contributing authors.

PAIRED\_KAMPFF. Published by Neto et al. (2016) and Marques-Smith et al. (2018), this study set provides in vivo recordings from the motor cortex of anaesthetised rats, pairing 32- and 128-channel dense silicon polytrodes with juxtacellular micro-pipettes. The source recordings are archived across two CRCNS.org deposits and are subject to the same terms as PAIRED\_CRCNS\_HC1: scientific use only, no public redistribution, with attribution required.

PAIRED\_MEA64C\_YGER. Published by Yger et al. (2018) and Spampinato et al. (2018), this is the sole ex vivo dataset in the collection, recorded from isolated mouse retinal tissue targeting retinal ganglion cells via simultaneous loose patch-clamp and a 252-channel MEA at 30 µm spacing. It is the only study set with a confirmed open licence, archived on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, permitting reuse and redistribution with attribution.

![][image2]

#### Hybrid simulation recordings

HYBRID\_JANELIA. The hybrid simulation study set, developed by Colonell and Pachitariu et al. (2019) at Janelia Research Campus and distributed via SpikeForest (Magland et al., 2020). We use this set of recordings as our source domain for the transfer learning. The simulation covers both sinusoidal and static drift conditions. 

The waveform used in the recordings originates from the Kampff lab. Even if no data leakage occurs at the recording level, full provenance and independence cannot be guaranteed. Therefore, we will not overestimate transfer learning claims on the Kampff family, as they might or might not share the same waveform.

### Datasets audit

Additionally, not all labelled paired rows have an fmiss label as we only define for units with an explicit ground truth match. We  consider a neuron matched only one of the neuron detected by the spike sorter has an accuracy score of at least 0.5 with the ground truth neuron. 

We require a valid match for fmiss because missed spikes can only be counted relative to a specific ground-truth neuron, whereas fpos can still be defined for an unmatched unit as the fraction of its assigned spikes that do not belong to any matched ground-truth source.

![][image3]  
Figure 2\. Dataset composition audit. Benchmarks combines a large labelled hybrid source domain, a smaller unlabelled paired domain, and a paired labelled domain of only 207 rows.

Our target fpos is available for each row. However, not every row has fmiss available. Therefore, we only train on test and paired data with fmiss available, but we include all rows, including those with missing fmiss, in our hybrid simulation dataset used during transfer learning.

Additionally, the difference between hybrid simulation and paired data is not only in the number of rows. Hybrid rows are more uniform and easier to handle, while paired rows are more realistic and are split internally into different families with varying recording methods and biological settings. These differences shape which model might be more suited for certain family types and why the final story cannot be reduced to a single model recipe. This is the reason why it is important to distinguish between generalizing across recordings of a family already present in training and generalising to unseen family recordings. 

## Feature construction

We built our dataset on derived features rather than raw voltage traces. We extracted features directly from Spikeforest recordings and sorting outputs. The feature packages is composed of waveform bins, autocorrelogram bins, amplitude statistics, SpikeInterface (citations) quality metrics, cosine similarity to compare to other neurons, and context about the recording.

### Waveform and autocorrelogram feature

The waveform of a neuron is the shape taken by the signal when this one fires.This waveform migh be of different amplitudes depending on the spike but it follow the neuron’s signature called a template. This template give us a lot of information about whether a specific spike might belong ot a certain neuron.

![][image4]  
Figure 3\. Here we can see two spike waveforms going through similar phases but with radically different templates. The different templates suggest they most likely come from different neurons, the right neurons having slower kinetics. 

Additionally, we compute cosine similarity with nearby neurons to identify potential spurious correlations arising from overlapping signals, which may hint at or model higher fpos or fmiss. 

On the other hand, an autocorrelogram allows us to analyse the temporal firing structure of a neuron. We analyse the distribution of spike occurrences across time lags relative to each other. It enables us to verify that our putative units do not break the biological refractory period. The refractory period is the interval following a spike in which a neuron is physiologically unable to fire again. A putative unit breaking it indicates that it contains overlapping signals from different neurons.  

![][image5]  
Figure 4\. The left panel shows a well-isolated single unit with a pronounced refractory period, indicating high sorting quality. Conversely, the right panel shows high refractory period violations, as indicated by the peak at 0, suggesting that uni is contaminated by an overlapping signal from multi-unit activity.

### To give our model access to waveform- and autocorrelogram-rich information, we discretised the signal into fixed bins. The waveform is divided into 30 different bins, while the autocorrelogram is discretised into 40 different bins, with its refractory period around the 20th bin.

![][image6]![][image7]![][image8]![][image9]![][image10]Figure 5\. The left graph compares the hybrid average waveform against each paired family’s average waveform. The hybrid waveform displays sharper edges and higher amplitude, making it easier to detect than the paired, smoother waveform. The autocorrelogram (ACGs) of hybrid shows perfect drop at the 20th bin, the refractory period, while paired ACGs show broader, noisier, and variable patterns.

### The discrepancy in ACGs betweend paired and hybrid suggest that the temporal firing statistics of real recordings are not correctly captured by  hybrid simulations. This highlights the domain shift between hybrid and paired recordings. 

### Additionally, it is worth highlighting that that even though the waveform of the Hybrid dataset are taken from Kampff laboratories (citation needed) their average waveform seems to be drastically different, comforting us in the low likelihood of a potential data leakage. 

Finally the paired family Boyden has a peak at the 20th bin, which is characteristic of bursting neuron which the Boyden family represents. Bursting neurons are neurons that fires rapid clusters of spikes, bursts, separated by periods of relative silence.

### Amplitude and amplitude stability features

Amplitude features describe how large the spikes are and amplitude stability how stable the size remains over time. These features are specific to each putative unit, for example, the mean, spread, quantiles, variability, and drift related changes of the amplitude in the recording. These features enable our model to analyse if the neuron’s spikes’ strength are consistent and if they fluctuate a lot over time. This gives our model clues about potential drift, poor isolation, or changing detectability, all of which are relevant to predict false positive and missed spikes. 

### Spike-timing summary statistics

In addition to the autocorrelogram, we implemented multiple features to enable our model to understand the spike-timing tendencies of our putative units. Example of such features are, firing rate, spike count, burst tendency, and refractory period violation rate.  These features capture how often a unit fires and how regular is it, and whether it stays consistent, capturing meaningful biological information to spot anomalies such as intermittent presence or excessive refractory period.

### SpikInterface quality control metrics

SpikeInterface (citation needed) is a standardised library to perform spike sorting end to end. In our case we used it to implement its reach quality control feature over our putative unit. We implemented their entire quality control package out of which are signal-to-noise ratio, drift summaries, and amplitude cutoff.  It allows our model to identify strong signal and stability across potential neurons. 

### Spatial Templates-footprint features

When a neuron spikes it is recorded and a probe with multiple channels its activity is recorded on multiple channel which makes that spikes overlap. Information about this spatial footprint such as the number of active channels, center of mass, and depth on the probe allow our model to understand where the spike is positioned with regards to the probe and how concentrated or diffuse its spatial footprint is. 

To visualise it, we plot the waveform received by every channel that captured the signal for the ground truth unit on a representation of the probe.   
![][image11]

Figure 6\. Example of a two units spatial footprint coming from Janelia’s hybrid simulation (citation needed). The average waveform of the unit on the left is represented clearly across the channels  its signal is captured, while the average waveform on the right seems to overlap with another unit on certain channels making it harder for the spike sorting algorithm. 

On the probe displaying ground truth unit 7, the template pattern is clear, and the peak amplitude decreases the further the signal leaves the peak channel. While on the other probe, where the signal of ground truth unit 98 is displayed, we see two channels having large amplitudes, while the shape of their waveform seems completely different. The presence of large-amplitude waveforms with distinct shapes across neighbouring channels may reflect either spike overlap between nearby neurons or differences in the spatial footprint of a single unit across the probe. In fact, the same neuron can appear biphasic in one channel and triphasic in another. Looking at a neuron's activity from different channels allows you to capture the full spectrum of its behaviour.

The information that spatial footprint features bring to our model is that units impacting multiple channels with overlapping spatial footprints are often harder to sort than others. 

### Isolation and confusability features

Another important important information to gather is how similar is each unit to its neighbouring units. Amongst features to do so, we developed cosine similarity features on waveforms and ACGs as well as other numerical variables. This helps build a feature counting the potential confusable neighbours. This feature family informs the model whether a unit is clearly distinct or resembles multiple units, and to what extent. By quantifying similarity continuously, it provides nuanced information that allows the model to weight fpos and fmiss accordingly.

### Recording-context features

In the modelling stage, we add context features to certain models to determine whether recording information helps the model adjust to differences between recordings and between paired families. These features include within-recording means, standard deviation, medians, interquartile ranges, deviations from the recording median, and percentile-rank versions of selected unit features. The benefit of these features is that they give the model a local baseline. The model is not judging the unit on absolute value, but also on whether it is abnormally large, noisy, stable, contaminated, or confusable relative to the other units in the recordings. This should be particularly useful against domain shift, as features can vary across studies, probes, sorters, and recording conditions.

## Matching units with ground truths In order to verify if the spike sorting algorithm correctly detected the ground truth unit we measure the model accuracy against a defined threshold. The accuracy is defined as:

### gt\_accuracy(u)=1−fpos(u)−fmiss(u)

### Where  for each ground-truth unit u:

* ### **fpos(u)** \= false positive rate (extra spikes wrongly assigned)

* ### **fmiss(u)** \= false negative rate (missed true spikes)

We then compare this accuracy against a chosen threshold that often ranges from 0.5 to 0.8. In our experiments, we set 0.5 to categorize well identified unit, but we still include best

## Model Families

### Stacking as the central design pattern

Stacking is an ensemble learning method introduced by  Wolpert (1992), where one or multiple first-stage models are used to build additional inputs for the second-stage learner. It is implemented by augmenting the dataset seen by the second-stage learner with predictions made by previous specialised models. These added features are often referred to as meta-features. Stacking works for both regression and classification tasks; it has been applied to regression by Breiman (1996) and to classification by LeBlanc and Tibshirani (1996).

As this problem relies on multiple sources of information, which differ both in nature and reliability, implementing stacking as our central design pattern makes it to add information from different sources for the final model to learn to use. Signals derived from the source domain, recording-level context, pseudo-labels from unlabeled paired data, and waveform-based representations each provide useful but imperfect evidence about unit quality. After the relevant meta-features are added to the dataset, the second stage learner, in our case, the model trained on labelled paired target domains, learns how much to trust each signal for a given unit. Treating intermediate predictions as fallible meta-features is especially relevant during an important domain shift, as source-derived predictions cannot be assumed to transfer uniformly to the labelled paired recordings domain.

### Baseline models

| Baseline model | Main data used | Role in the benchmark |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Dummy paired mean | Paired labeled only | Sanity-floor predictor that always returns the target mean of the paired training set |
| Paired-only raw XGboost | Paired labeled only | Target-only reference model using raw unit-level features without source transfer |
| Hybrid-only XGBoost | Hybrid labeled only | Source-only transfer reference model used to measure the raw cost of domain shift |

### Retained first stage configurations

Table below groups the core stacked benchmark recipes by the actual first-stage configuration they expose to the second-stage learner. 

* **source\_pred** — a scalar regression prediction produced by a paired-domain LightGBM teacher trained on labeled target rows, using full context alongside a raw importance-weighted hybrid prediction. Out-of-fold and held-out predictions are propagated forward as a transferred first guess of the target metric (fpos or fmiss), compactly encoding what a source-informed teacher believes about each unit. It provides the second stage with an initial estimate of the outcome, so the final model can start from an informed prediction instead of having to infer everything from scratch.  
* **anchor\_fp\_score** — a scalar probability in \[0, 1\] from a gradient-boosted classifier trained to distinguish labeled matched rows from unlabeled paired-pool rows, using masked context and unit features. It acts as a global "unlabeled-pool likeness" score, indicating how much a unit resembles the structured unlabeled pool rather than labeled training data. It provides information about whether the unit looks like the broader population the model may encounter at deployment, which is useful because a unit can be realistic and important even if it is not well represented in the labeled set.  
* **matched\_support\_conf** — a scalar confidence in \[0, 1\] derived from a PCA-based neighborhood support model that converts distance to labeled neighbors into an exponentially decaying confidence. It is a local support signal: high values indicate strong similarity to labeled target data, while low values flag sparse or unsupported regions. It provides a measure of how much nearby labeled evidence exists for this unit, meaning whether the model is making a prediction in a familiar region with close known examples or in a more isolated region where transfer is less certain.  
* **anchor\_support\_margin** — computed directly as anchor\_fp\_score − matched\_support\_conf. This signed scalar captures disagreement between global and local structure: positive values mean a unit is both unlabeled-pool-like and locally unsupported, while negative values indicate it is well anchored in the labeled neighborhood. It provides a simple summary of tension between "this looks like real unlabeled data" and "this is well supported by labeled examples," which helps identify cases that may be realistic but still hard to predict because they are weakly covered by supervision.  
* **wf\_embed\_\*** — a low-dimensional vector learned by a convolutional autoencoder trained on waveform bins from hybrid and non-test paired data. It provides a compact representation of spike morphology, capturing structure absent from handcrafted tabular features. It provides shape-based information about the waveform itself, which is useful when biologically meaningful differences between units are visible in morphology but are not fully captured by standard summary features.

## Model recipes

The retained compared models can be stated directly in recipe form. These recipes differ not only in their learner family, but also in which first-stage signals are exposed to the second-stage model and in whether additional unlabeled or waveform-derived information is introduced.

* Paired-only context: This model uses only leakage-safe target-context features and does not append any source-derived first-stage outputs. It is therefore the pure target-context control for both fpos and fmiss, allowing the contribution of stacked transfer signals to be evaluated against a context-only target-domain baseline.  
* Context-first source stack: This is the canonical non-neural stack for fpos. It passes source\_pred, anchor\_fp\_score, matched\_support\_conf, and anchor\_support\_margin to the second-stage learner, together with the target-context feature table. Methodologically, it serves as the reference structured stack before pseudo-labeled unlabeled rows or waveform embeddings are introduced.  
* Reduced-latent context: This retained fmiss variant keeps only source\_pred and anchor\_fp\_score, while dropping the support-derived columns matched\_support\_conf and anchor\_support\_margin. Its role is to test whether the most portable transfer signals remain useful in a more compact stacked formulation, without requiring the full anchor/support signal set.  
* Pre-waveform unlabeled structure: This fpos recipe uses the same four transfer columns as the context-first source stack, but the second-stage learner is additionally trained on selected pseudo-labeled unlabeled rows that pass the trust filter. Its distinctive feature is therefore not a different first-stage column set, but a different second-stage training procedure that incorporates structured unlabeled paired data.  
* Waveform-augmented structure: This final retained fpos recipe extends the full anchor/support stack by appending learned wf\_embed\_\* coordinates as additional second-stage covariates. It combines the tabular transfer structure with learned waveform morphology, and should therefore be interpreted as the anchor/support stack plus an explicit waveform representation rather than as a separate learning path.

Model are evaluated on 20 different seeds which allows us to evaluate their performance on different dataset splits  for recording disjoint seed. Evaluating on multiple seeds also affects model stochastocoty and pseudo-label selection, which impacts both recording disjoint and LOFO splits.

## Metrics

The two main metrics we are optimising our models for are R-squared and Mean Average Error. R-squared is fundamental as it allow us to explain how much of the variance does our model explain, providing a global measure of its explanatory power. The mean average error on the other measure how far our predictions are from the ground truth, making it easy to interpret the typical size of the error.

As we run our model on 20 different seeds we aggregate the mean R-squared and MAE of each model across seed to account for model stochasticity and preferable dataset splits.

## Data leakage prevention

The anti-leakage policy is not only conceptual but strictly enforced throughout the benchmark implementation. A recording\_key, constructed from the study set and recording name, is used as the fundamental grouping unit for both the main train–test split and all validation procedures. The data pipeline explicitly separates the dataset into four disjoint pools: hybrid source data, paired fine-tuning data, paired test data, and an unlabeled target pool built exclusively from non-test recordings. Safeguards ensure that no overlap exists between held-out recordings and either the fine-tuning or unlabeled pools. This constraint is consistently reapplied during grouped validation, where pseudo-labeled rows originating from a validation recording are excluded whenever that recording is used for evaluation.

These precautions are especially critical for stack-based models, where features such as recording-level context statistics, pseudo-label support estimates, and trust scores encode strong recording-specific structure. While powerful, such features are treated as potentially unsafe and are only permitted when they do not violate the train–test boundary. In practice, the benchmark enforces a strict rule: any feature that could not be computed at deployment time for a truly unseen recording must not be used during model selection. At the split-construction level, group-aware shuffling replaces naive row sampling, generating candidate splits over recording groups and selecting the one that best balances two competing constraints: maintaining strict recording isolation while preserving a sufficiently large and stable labeled test set in this inherently label-scarce setting.

### Reproducibility measures

The project was written as a thesis-facing research package rather than a one-off notebook directory, and several reproducibility measures follow from that choice:

* **Frozen inputs and tracked outputs.** The thesis is written against frozen input bundles and tracked figure/table outputs, rather than informal notebook screenshots.  
* **Recipe registry.** The runnable experiment catalog under qc\_thesis.modeling.recipes defines the source of truth for the benchmarked models and avoids undocumented recipe drift.  
* **Environment capture.** The repository includes a conda environment file and a generated environment snapshot recording the Python version, platform, git commit, branch, and environment metadata used for a thesis-facing run.  
* **Auditing.** The audit\_thesis\_package.py script checks that required directories exist, that notebooks use the thesis-root bootstrap rather than ad hoc working-directory logic, that cache directories are absent when requested, and that the recipe registry is internally valid.  
* **Explicit freeze path.** The reproducibility README documents the final command sequence for rebuilding the robustness sweep, notebooks, figures, and environment snapshot.

These steps do not imply that the project is fully one-command reproducible from raw SpikeForest extraction. The original extraction depended on external services and Colab-specific runtime behavior. What the thesis does provide is an explicit and auditable path from the frozen packaged dataset to the manuscript-facing results.

# 

# Results

## The transfer problem is real

The primary finding of the thesis is that the domain shift from hybrid simulation data to paired juxtacellular recording is significant. In fact, they are easily separable, as a domain classifier trained to differentiate source data from target data achieves an area under the curve of 0.976 without recording context features and 0.9997 with them. This indicates that the source and target domains are almost linearly separable based on the features available to the model. 

| Comparison | Feature set | Mean AUC | Std. dev. |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Hybrid vs paired (all) | Unit | 0.9765 | 0.0463 |
| Hybrid vs paired (all) | Full context | 0.9997 | 0.0005 |

![][image13]  
Figure 8\. Comparison of feature distributions for six key features, highlighting domain shift

This separability is supported by the distribution shift, as shown by features that carry very strong signals about a unit’s composition. Additionally, recording-context variables have a mean absolute standardized mean difference of about 0.518, waveform bins about 0.711, and the broader “other” unit block about 0.734. This again highlights the complexity of paired recording, which exhibits higher noise, contamination, and instability. This reinforces our assumption of H1.

The two-dimensional principal-component projection confirms a similar pattern.  
![][image14]![][image15]  
            (a) paired family only                                       (b) Hybrid vs paired  
Figure 4.2: Two-dimensional PCA views of the benchmark feature space. The target domain is internally heterogeneous rather than being a single compact cluster.

The paired target domain should be thought of as a set of related sub-regimes rather than a compact distribution. English spreads across most of the local PCA view, which is consistent with its biological diversity, as its recordings target three different brain regions: hippocampus, neocortex, and thalamus. Kampff occupies a more displaced region, highlighting a structural difference from other paired families. Finally, MEA64C\_Yger is relatively compact.

## Fpos: Positive transfer stories exist

The main fpos benchmark using the retained models was assessed using the recording-disjoint method across 20 seeds from 42 to 61\. As expected, the dummy floor’s R-squared remains very close to 0, at \-0.05. The highest overall mean R-squared is achieved by the paired-only raw model with 0.4209. The hybrid-only source transfer baseline dropped to \-1.8162, as anticipated following the previously identified significant domain shift. The paired domain contains a notable predictive signal, but naive source transfer is unsafe.   
Among the models combining source-side information, some closely matched the paired-only raw R-squared, indicating effective transfer. However, while the R-squared does not collapse, it did not bring significant general improvement either. Paired-only context reaches 0.4188 R', the context-first source stack 0.3973, the pre-waveform unlabeled structure stack 0.4068, and waveform-augmented structure 0.3906.   
![][image16]  
Figure 9\. Mean R-squared across 20 seeds (42-61) with a recording disjoint split. The model's results showed very close performance rather than a single universal winner.  
Mean R-squared, however, does not show the full picture. Looking at the mean average square error, the pre-waveform unlabeled structure is the best-performing one with 13.02. The story is similar for MAE: most models extract a real signal score in the low 0.13 range rather than a single clear best performer.  Additionally,  pre-waveform unlabeled structure is also the model with the highest mean rank, 2.40/5, and the highest among of seed wins, seed where the model had the highest R-squared, with 5 wins out of 20\.   
![][image17]

Figure 9\. Fpos best performing across 20 seeds (42-61) with held out recordings. The robustness of a model does not imply performance on single splits.

Taken together, these results support a positive transfer narrative for fpos without indicating a universal model winner. Moreover, split-average stability matters as much as the strongest single split, as it conveys a model's robustness. Even though the paired-only raw model has the highest R-squared and the second-lowest average MAE, it is the model with the lowest mean rank among the best-performing models. Suggesting that the meta-features allow performance to depend on the specific split of units available at training and test, with sixteen out of twenty times one of those models getting a higher R-squared than the robust paired-only raw.

## Family preferences explain part of the instability

Analysing models' performance across different families using the leave-one-family-out (LOFO) protocol, in which no data from the family are seen during training and the entire family is evaluated during testing, is the most rigorous way to assess cross-family generalisation.   
![][image18]

Figure 10\. Held out family fpos mean R-squared heatmap across twenty different seeds (42-61).

Under that held-out-family benchmark, BOYDEN, KAMPFF, and MEA64C\_YGER prefer the waveform-augmented structure model; CRCNS\_HC1 prefers the paired-only context model; and ENGLISH slightly prefers the context-first source stack. However, the model waveform-augmented feature seems to perform best overall, ranking first across three families.

These preferences give relevant information; they should be read carefully, taking into account the nature of datasets as well as the biological context. The performance differences between families are striking. Kampff’s best model, waveform-augmented structure, achieves an average R-squared of 0.71 across 20 seeds. This strongly suggests that the model captures stable and informative structure in this family. However, the best model of the Boyden family, also a waveform-augmented structure, averages an R-squared of 0.14.   
![][image19]

## Fmiss: the models do not yet deliver a robot's transfer story

The models compared in fmiss differ from the one studies in fpos. This is intentional as we tried using a similar model, but fmiss transfer configurations collapse or produce noisy predictions. Those models were not informative. In fact, fmiss is more global, tied to other putative units,  and firing dynamics. Using the same models for both targets would lead to non-informative comparisons. Therefore, each target is instead evaluated on its meaningful models.
